title: Sleep or journey
hookLine: Socrates, just sentenced to death: it is either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and neither is to be feared

cards: The vote has just been counted. An Athenian jury has sentenced an old man to death for corrupting the young and failing to honor the city's gods. A person might rage, or beg, or go silent.

Socrates turns to the jurors who voted to acquit him and says, in effect: stay a minute, friends, let's talk while the officials are busy. And what he wants to talk about is the thing just handed to him.
In Plato's account of the trial, the Apology, he lays out two possibilities for what death is, two doors, and walks through neither.

teach.b: First, a silence he trusts. Socrates says an inner sign has all his life stopped him when he was about to do wrong, even in small things.
That day it never stopped him: not leaving home, not walking into court, not in his speech. He takes its silence as a hint that what is happening may be good.
Second, the first door: sleep. Maybe death is nothing at all, no awareness, like a night of sleep without even a dream.

Think of your best night of deep sleep, he tells the jurors, and set it against all the other days and nights of your life. Even the great king of Persia, he says, would find few days and nights better.
If death is like that, he says, it is a gain.
Third, the second door: a journey. Maybe death is a move to another place, where the dead are. Then he would meet the poets and heroes of old and keep asking questions, testing who is wise.
And there, he jokes, they surely don't put you to death for asking. Fourth, either way. Socrates doesn't claim to know which door is real.
His point is that neither gives a reason to be afraid.

He tells them a good person has nothing evil to fear, in life or after death. And he ends: now it's time to go, I to die and you to live, and which of us goes to the better thing, only God knows. That is Plato's Socrates.
Others in this block will answer differently, on their own days.

how: Students of philosophy read Socrates's closing words in Plato's Apology as an example of facing death with reasoning rather than fear, without claiming to know what death is.

o: a trance used to reach the world of the dead
Socrates's picture of death as a sleep with no dream
the Greek god who ferries the dead across a river

games.q: Socrates after the verdict — tap the pairs.
p: a sleep without even a dream
a journey to meet the dead

s: Socrates claimed to know which of the two was true
he set out both and said neither gives reason to fear.
he spoke these words after he had been sentenced
in the Apology he talks with the jurors who voted to acquit him.
he said a dreamless sleep would be a loss
he said that if death is like that, it is a gain.

games.q: you are Socrates. the jury has just sentenced you to death. the officials are busy. what do you do?
o: talk calmly with your friends about what death might be.
games.why: he stays to talk, sets out two possibilities, and finds a reason to fear in neither.

practice: Take the first door: think of the deepest sleep you can remember, the kind where no time seemed to pass, and rest there a few breaths.

Then take the second: a long trip, a new place, people you've wanted to meet, and rest there too. Hold both without choosing, and notice whether fear shows up in either; if this is tender today, rest in the breath instead.

wordCard.voice: Hypnos, Socrates's first picture of death in Plato's Apology: a sleep with no dream, no cause for fear. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: hypnos, sleep. Socrates's first picture of death in the Apology is a sleep with no dream.

carryVoice: Your line: either way. Two doors, and fear behind neither. Day seven hundred sixty, done.
